DOUBLE FILTRATION PLASMA EXCHANGE AND
IMMUNOADSORPTION THERAPY IN A CASE
OF STIFF-MAN SYNDROME WITH NEGATIVE ANTI-GAD
ANTIBODY
Akito Hayashi, Kiyotaka Nakamagoe, Norio Ohkoshi,
Sachiko Hoshino and Shin'ichi Shoji
Department of Neurology, Institute of Clinical Medicine,
University of Tsukuba, Tsukuba-city, Ibaraki-ken, 305-8575, Japan
Key Words; Anti-GAD antibody, double filtration plasma exchange,
immunoadsorption therapy, stiff-man syndrome,
Subjects: Male patient
Abbreviations: GAD = glutamic acid decarboxylase.
Abstract
We report the effects of double filtration plasma exchange and
immunoadsorption therapy which were performed for a case of stiff-man
syndrome even though the patient was negative for anti-glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD) antibody. The patient underwent a course of four
double filtration plasma exchanges, which resulted in marked clinical
improvement. Painful muscle cramps disappeared and muscle stiffness
reduced a day after the first plasma exchange. The patient's
improvement continued, but his condition declined again about ten
months after plasma exchange. Immunoadsorption therapy was then
performed, and this treatment was also effective.
Introduction
Stiff-man syndrome is a very rare disorder characterized by
continuous muscular stiffness and painful muscle cramps (Gordon,

treatment with diazepam (Lorish, Thorsteinsson ef al., 1989), baclofen
(Miller and Korsvik, 1981; Whelan, 1980), clonazepam (Westbrom,
1977), sodium valproate (Spehimann, Noreross ef al., 1981) or clonidine
(Meinck, Ricker ef al., 1984). The cause of the stiff-man syndrome is
still obscure, but Solimena, Folli ef al. (1988, 1990) observed
autoantibodies to GABAergic neurons in 20 of 32 patients with the
disorder and suggested that GAD is the primary autoantigen. Vicari, Folli
et al. (1989) first reported the effect of plasmapheresis in stiff-man
syndrome with anti-GAD antibody. We evaluated the effects of double
filtration plasma exchange and immunoadsorption which were performed
for a case of stiff-man syndrome, and found that the treatment was
effective in spite of negative findings for anti-GAD antibody.
Case Report
A 57-year-old man developed symptoms of painful stiffness of
his back and limbs, muscle cramps, and difficulty in walking in 1984. He
first came under a doctor's care in 1984 because of symptoms of his skin
and was diagnosed as progressive dermatosclerosis with muscle cramps.
He was treated with prednisolone (25 mg daily) and diazepam (30 mg
daily) at a hospital, which reduced symptoms to some extent. Despite
continued administration of the drugs, however, his symptoms gradually
began to worsen, and he was admitted to our hospital in December 1994,
There was no family history of neuromuscular disease or diabetes
mellitus, He had undergone surgery for an early-stage lung cancer
(adenocarcinoma) with early stage at the age of $1 years and suffered
from left cerebral thrombosis at the age of 53 years, Physical
examination revealed local dermatosclerosis on his arms, a scar from his
operation on his chest, and hyperhidrosis. Neurological examination
showed that his mental state, cranial nerves, and cerebellar functions
were normal other than slight right hemiparesis with hemisensory
disturbance due to left cerebral thrombosis. There was continuous
stiffness in his four limbs and truncal muscles. The stiffness or increased
muscle tone was influenced by his momentary emotional state: it
increased when he was under stress, decreased when he was relaxed or
drowsy, and disappeared during sleep. He had difficulty in walking and
standing. Limb movements were severely disturbed by muscle stiffness
and finger movement was clumsy. Ocular movements and swallowing
were normal, Painful generalized muscle cramps were easily elicited by

were fixed in flexion posture and lower limbs in extension posture, His
trunk was as stiff as wood and his face was grimaced under the
unbearable pain. Laboratory tests revealed no abnormal findings in sugar

smooth-muscle antibody were positive. Immunocytochemical study of

Discussion
Our patient was diagnosed as stiff-man syndrome from his
characteristic features: i.e., muscular stiffness and cramps. The cause of
stiff-man syndrome is still obscure, but Solimena, Folli e¢ al. (1988)
observed autoantibodies to GABAergic neurons in about 60% of patients
with the disorder and suggested that GAD is the primary autoantigen,
Some patients with stiff-man syndrome and breast cancer who
had negative anti-GAD antibodies had autoantibodies against a 128-kd
neuronal protein (Bussel and Pirerrot-Deseilligny, 1977). Our patient had
been operated on for an early-stage lung cancer five years before, but no
malignancy was detected at the time of admission. Although the
immunocytochemical study for antineuronal autoantibodies was neg;
in our patient, an anti-DNA antibody, antinuclear antibody, and anti-
smooth-muscle antibody were positive. These findings suggested that a
paraneoplastic mechanism could not be considered in our patient.
So far, the disorder is known to respond to treatment with
diazepam (Lorish, Thorsteinsson ef ai, 1989), baclofen (Miller, and
Korsvik, 1981; Whelan, 1980), clonazepam (Westbrom, 1977), sodium
valproate (Spehlmann, Norcross et al., 1981) or clonidine (Meinck,
Ricker er al., 1984). In our patient, diazepam and prednisolone improved
the symptoms, but the effect was insufficient, Vicari, Folli et al. (1989)
first reported the effect of plasma exchange with prednisolone in stiff
man syndrome with anti-GAD antibody; a number of similar cases have
been reported since (Brashear and Phillips, 1991; Harding, Thompson et
al., 1989; Meinck, Ricker ef a/., 1994). Even though our patient was
negative for anti-GAD antibody, we decided to attempt treatment with
double filtration plasma exchange and immunoadsorption. The patient
showed marked clinical improvement by the treatments. The effect of
plasma exchange continued for about ten months and the
325

immunoadsorption therapy showed effects similar to those of the
previous plasma exchange. These findings suggest that autoimmune
disorder existed in our patient even though antineuronal autoantibodies
were not detected. Meinck, Ricker ef al. (1994) also described one case
with negative GAD antibodies which responded favorably to plasma
exchange.
It appears likely, therefore, that our case had an unknown
antibody, and that stiffman syndrome is heterogenous. Clinically, a
doctor should attempt treatment with plasma exchange or immuno-
adsorption even in cases with stiff:man syndrome with negative
antineuronal antibodies.

We thank Dr. M. Solimena and Prof. P. De Camilli for measuring
anti-GAD autoantibodies by immunocytochemical study.

been reported since (Brashear and Phillips, 1991; Harding, Thompson et
al., 1989; Meinck, Ricker ef a/., 1994). Even though our patient was
negative for anti-GAD antibody, we decided to attempt treatment with
double filtration plasma exchange and immunoadsorption. The patient
showed marked clinical improvement by the treatments. The effect of

immunoadsorption therapy showed effects similar to those of the
previous plasma exchange. These findings suggest that autoimmune
disorder existed in our patient even though antineuronal autoantibodies
were not detected. Meinck, Ricker ef al. (1994) also described one case
with negative GAD antibodies which responded favorably to plasma
exchange.
It appears likely, therefore, that our case had an unknown
antibody, and that stiffman syndrome is heterogenous. Clinically, a
doctor should attempt treatment with plasma exchange or immuno-
adsorption even in cases with stiff:man syndrome with negative
antineuronal antibodies.
